prompt: `Desk`'s loop called `item.describe()` on three elements declared `Item`. What did it print?
hint: Each object ran its own override.

choices.why: That would mean the declared type chose the body; it chooses only what may be called.
Right: one call in the source, three bodies at run time.

choices.text: A compile error, since `Item` cannot hold a `Book`
choices.why: A variable may hold any subclass of its type.

prompt: `Item item = new Book(...)` followed by `item.isbn()` does not compile. Why, when the object is a book?
hint: What does the compiler look at?

choices.why: It is public; the error said the symbol could not be found.

choices.text: Because the object was converted to an `Item` when it was assigned
choices.why: Assignment changes nothing about the object; it is still a `Book`.
Right: the compiler checks declarations only; what the object really is becomes known at run time.

prompt: `(Book) items[1]` compiled, and the program then threw `ClassCastException`. What does that say about a cast?
hint: Who checked the promise, and when?

choices.text: It moves the check to run time, when the cast executes
choices.why: Right: the compiler accepts a cast that could succeed, and the JVM checks the real class.

choices.text: It converts the object into the target class
choices.why: Nothing was converted: a `Dvd` stays a `Dvd`, so the cast failed.

choices.text: It turns off type checking for that line
choices.why: The JVM checked, and refused.

choices.text: It is a compile error that `javac` only reports when the program runs
choices.why: Compile errors are reported by `javac`; this one compiled.

prompt: Which form does the section recommend for using `isbn()` on an `Item` that might be a book?
hint: The one that turns a crash into a branch.

choices.why: If the item is a DVD, that throws.
Right: it asks first, and names the result.

choices.text: Add `isbn()` to `Item`, returning `null` for anything else
choices.why: That gives every item a method that means nothing for most of them.

prompt: On which line of `Casts.java` did the `ClassCastException` happen?
hint: The last line of the stack trace.

prompt: In `say`, which method does the `invokevirtual` instruction name?
hint: The compiler wrote what it knew.

choices.text: `Book.describe`, since the first call passes a book
choices.why: `say` is compiled once and called with both; it cannot name one subclass.
Right: the declared type, with the body left open.
`describe` is declared in `Item`, and that is what is named.

choices.text: None; it names a slot number in a table
choices.why: The instruction names a method; the table is how HotSpot looks it up.

prompt: When `invokevirtual Item.describe` runs on a `Dvd`, how does the JVM find the body?
hint: It starts from the object.

choices.text: It runs `Item.describe`, since that is the method the instruction names
choices.why: The name says which method; the object's class says which body.

choices.text: It asks the compiler, which recorded the answer in the class file
choices.why: The compiler is long gone at run time and recorded only the declared type.

choices.text: It reads the object's class and looks the method up in that class's table
choices.why: Right: `Dvd`'s table maps `describe` to `Dvd.describe`.

prompt: Which instruction calls a method through an interface type, such as lesson 23's `Lendable`?
hint: Its name says it.

choices.why: That is for static methods, chosen by the compiler.
Right: dispatched by the object's class, like `invokevirtual`.

prompt: A colleague avoids small overridable methods "because virtual calls are slow". What does the section answer?
hint: The JIT watches each call site.

choices.text: That the colleague is right, and `final` everywhere is the remedy
choices.why: The section argues the opposite: it is a design decision.

choices.text: That a look-up is cheap, and the JIT calls one class directly where it has seen only one
choices.why: Right: so the choice is about design, not speed.

choices.text: That the JVM searches up to `Object` on every call, which is fast enough
choices.why: HotSpot does not search on every call; each class has a table.

prompt: Which kind of member follows the object, as `who()` did?
hint: Only one of the four did.

choices.why: `p.name` printed `parent field`: bound by the declared type.
`p.kind()` printed `parent static`.
Right: the only kind that dispatches.
`callSecret()` printed `parent private`.

prompt: `Parent p = new Child();` and `Child` declares its own `name`. What does `p.name` read, and why?
hint: Look at the `getfield` instruction.

choices.text: `child field`, because the object behind the variable is a `Child`
choices.why: Fields do not dispatch; the object's class plays no part.
Right: two fields share the name, and the declared type picked one.

choices.text: A compile error, since two fields cannot share a name
choices.why: Hiding a field is legal, which is why it surprises.

prompt: `callSecret()` in `Parent` calls `secret()`, and `Child` also has a private `secret()`. Why did a `Child` object print `parent private`?
hint: Can a subclass see a private method?

choices.text: Because the call was compiled as `invokestatic`
choices.why: `javap` showed `invokevirtual`; the instruction is not the reason.
Adding it would be a compile error: there is nothing to override.
Right: a private method is never overridden, so the JVM selects `Parent`'s, and `Child.secret` is an unrelated method with the same name.

prompt: `p.kind()` printed `parent static` because the compiler wrote `___ Parent.kind`.
hint: The instruction for static methods.

prompt: Which of these are bound by the compiler, from the declared type? Choose all that apply.
hint: Everything except overridable instance methods.

choices.why: Yes: `getfield` names the class.
Yes: `invokestatic`.

choices.text: Calling a public instance method that a subclass overrides
choices.why: No: that is dynamic dispatch.
Yes: `invokespecial`, exactly the one named.

prompt: `Item[] items = { new Book(...) }; Book b = (Book) items[0]; Item i = b;` Then `i.describe()` and `b.describe()`. What do they print?
hint: One object, two variables.

choices.why: The method follows the object, whatever variable you call it through.

choices.text: `a book`, twice, from the one object

The element really is a `Book`, so the cast succeeds.

prompt: A `Report` class has `public static String header()`, and `DetailedReport extends Report` declares its own `header()`. Code calls `report.header()` with `Report report = new DetailedReport();` and expects the detailed header. What is the fix?
hint: Static methods do not dispatch.

choices.why: On a static method that is a compile error, not a fix.
It works and spreads knowledge of the subclass into every caller.
Right: make `header()` an instance method in both classes; then it overrides, and the object chooses.

items: The JVM reads the class of the object `item` refers to

prompt: Why does the section say a static method should be called on its class's name, never through a variable?
hint: What did `p.kind()` suggest, and what did it do?

choices.text: It looks dynamic and is not
choices.why: Right: through a variable it looks as if the object chooses; `Parent.kind()` says what really happens.

choices.text: Because calling it through a variable is a compile error
choices.why: It compiled and ran; it only misleads.

choices.text: Because it is slower through a variable
